content.text: King Aswapati of the Madras, childless and grown old, spent eighteen years in austerities and daily oblations honoring the goddess Savitri, praying for offspring. Pleased, the goddess appeared to him in embodied form from the sacrificial fire and granted that a daughter of great energy would be born to him. When she came, the king and Brahmanas named her Savitri after the goddess by whose favor she had been given.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: As Savitri grew, her radiance was such that no man dared ask for her hand. Grieved that no suitor came forward, her father told her: "None asketh thee. Do thou therefore thyself seek for a husband equal to thee in qualities!" Bowing to her father, she set out in a golden car with his aged counsellors to travel the forest hermitages of the sages in search of a husband of her own choosing.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: Savitri chose Satyavan, the exiled and blind King Dyumatsena's son, living a hermit's life in the forest -- though the sage Narada had warned that Satyavan was fated to die within the year. Undeterred, she held to her choice, and her father formally gave her in marriage. Putting off her royal ornaments for bark-cloth, she served her husband and his aged parents with such devotion that everyone in the hermitage was pleased by her, even as Narada's warning stayed present in her mind day and night.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: On the foretold day, Satyavan felt a splitting pain in his head while gathering wood in the forest and laid his head in Savitri's lap to rest. She saw Yama himself, dreadful of aspect with noose in hand, standing over her husband. Yama drew Satyavan's life out of his body "of the measure of a thumb, bound in noose," and the body lay lifeless. Then he turned south to depart -- and Savitri, grief-stricken, rose and followed him.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: Yama told her to turn back and perform her husband's funeral rites, saying she had come as far as any mortal could. Savitri answered: "Whither my husband is being carried, or whither he goeth of his own accord, I will follow him thither. This is the eternal custom." She continued walking beside Yama, speaking to him of virtue, true knowledge, and the company of the righteous with such grace and wisdom that Yama, delighted, offered her boon after boon -- excepting only her husband's life.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: Savitri asked, in turn: her blind father-in-law's eyesight restored, his lost kingdom returned, a hundred sons for her own father, and finally -- "Both of me and Satyavan's loins, begotten by both of us, let there be a century of sons" -- a boon Yama granted without noticing it could not be fulfilled while Satyavan remained dead. She then pointed this out plainly: "The boon thou hast already given me is incapable of accomplishment without union with my husband... May Satyavan be restored to life, for by that thy words will be made true." Yama, bound by his own word, untied the noose and freed Satyavan's life.
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli

content.text: Every boon Savitri won came to pass: Dyumatsena regained his sight and, soon after, his throne; Satyavan and Savitri lived together for four hundred years and had a hundred sons who became renowned kings. The sage Markandeya, closing the tale for Yudhishthira, declared: "The man that listeneth with reverence to the excellent story of Savitri, attaineth to happiness, and success in everything, and never meeteth with misery!"
content.source_name: The Mahabharata, Book 3: Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva, tr. K.M. Ganguli
